title: Concerning rent stabilization by limiting the frequency and amount of rent increases.
summary: Statewide rent control legislation that caps annual rent increases. Prohibits landlords from raising rent more than once per year and limits the amount of increase. Supporters argue it protects tenants from displacement; opponents warn it will reduce housing supply and discourage new construction.
supporters: Tenant advocacy groups, housing justice organizations, low-income advocates
opponents: Rental housing associations, real estate developers, small landlords
provisions: Limits frequency of rent changes to once per year
fullSummary: This is the most significant housing legislation of the 2025 session. It establishes statewide rent stabilization for the first time in Washington history. The bill passed on party-line votes in both chambers with narrow margins. Legal challenges are expected from property rights groups. Implementation begins January 2026.

title: Concerning the taxation of capital gains and estates by creating a more progressive rate structure.
summary: Increases capital gains tax from 7% to 9.9% on earnings over $1M. Raises estate tax rates up to 15% and lowers exemption threshold. Generates approximately $2.9 billion in new revenue for education funding.
supporters: Education funding advocates, labor unions, progressive tax groups
opponents: Business associations, wealth managers, estate planners, tech industry
provisions: Estate tax rate increases up to 15%
Revenue directed to education legacy trust
fullSummary: Major tax legislation that significantly increases taxes on high earners and estates. The capital gains portion targets tech executives and investors. Estate tax changes affect family farms and businesses. Revenue funds K-12 and higher education. Republicans uniformly opposed; Democrats split on estate tax provisions.

title: Concerning firearm safety by requiring a permit to purchase firearms.
summary: Requires Washington State Patrol background check and five-year permit for all firearm purchases. Includes safety training requirement and waiting period. One of the most significant gun safety laws in state history.
supporters: Gun safety advocates, law enforcement, domestic violence prevention groups
opponents: Gun rights groups, Second Amendment advocates, rural gun owners
watchers: Firearms dealers, shooting ranges, hunting organizations
provisions: Permit required for all firearm purchases
fullSummary: Landmark gun safety legislation creating a permit-to-purchase system. Similar laws exist in only a handful of states. Implementation requires significant WSP infrastructure development. Legal challenges expected on Second Amendment grounds. Takes effect July 2026 with phased implementation.

title: Concerning consumer protection by prohibiting the reporting of medical debt to consumer credit reporting agencies.
summary: Prohibits healthcare providers and collection agencies from reporting medical debt to credit bureaus. Protects consumers from credit score damage due to medical expenses. First-in-nation comprehensive medical debt credit protection.
supporters: Consumer protection groups, healthcare advocates, patient rights organizations
opponents: Debt collection industry, credit reporting agencies, some healthcare providers
provisions: Prohibition on medical debt credit reporting
fullSummary: Nation-leading consumer protection law that removes medical debt from credit reports. Affects approximately 750,000 Washingtonians with medical debt on credit reports. Collection industry argues it reduces payment incentives. Healthcare providers concerned about revenue collection. Implementation January 2026.

title: Concerning paid family and medical leave by expanding eligibility and benefits.
summary: Expands Paid Family and Medical Leave program by eliminating exemptions, lowering eligibility thresholds, and increasing benefits. Adds administrative requirements for employers.
supporters: Labor unions, worker advocacy groups, family caregivers
opponents: Small business associations, employer groups, chambers of commerce
watchers: HR professionals, payroll companies, large employers
fullSummary: Major expansion of Washington's PFML program, one of the most generous in the nation. Small businesses previously exempt now must participate. Employers face increased administrative burden and payroll costs. Labor groups celebrate as major worker victory. Effective January 2026.

title: Concerning transportation funding by increasing the motor vehicle fuel tax and establishing new fees.
summary: 6-cent per gallon gas tax increase bringing total state tax to 55.4 cents. Adds luxury vehicle tax, tire disposal fee, and automatic 2% annual inflation adjustment. Funds transportation infrastructure projects.
supporters: Transportation advocates, infrastructure groups, transit supporters
opponents: Anti-tax groups, drivers, rural residents, trucking industry
watchers: EV manufacturers, alternative fuel industry, municipal governments
fullSummary: Controversial transportation funding package. Gas tax increase hits rural drivers hardest who drive longer distances. Automatic inflation adjustment ensures revenue grows without legislative votes. EV owners largely exempt, creating equity concerns. Funds bridge repairs, highway maintenance, and transit expansion.

title: Concerning unemployment insurance by providing benefits to striking workers.
summary: Provides up to 6 weeks of unemployment benefits to workers on strike. Makes Washington one of few states with strike benefits. Significant win for organized labor.
supporters: Labor unions, worker advocacy groups, Democratic legislators
fullSummary: Historic labor legislation making Washington one of first states to provide strike benefits. Business groups argue it incentivizes strikes and drains UI fund. Labor calls it essential worker protection. Excludes police and firefighters. Takes effect July 2025.

title: Concerning business and occupation taxes by adjusting rates for certain business activities.
summary: Increases B&O tax rates for certain service industries while creating exemptions for others. Targeted tax increase on professional services, tech, and consulting. Part of broader revenue package.
supporters: Education funding advocates, progressive groups, labor
opponents: Small businesses, service industry, tech sector, professional services
provisions: B&O rate increases for service categories
fullSummary: Complex B&O tax restructuring that increases rates on high-margin service businesses while protecting small businesses. Tech industry particularly affected. Part of $9.4 billion tax package to address budget deficit. Implementation staggered to reduce shock.

title: Concerning corporations by making technical updates to the Washington business corporation act.
summary: Technical updates to Washington's corporation and nonprofit acts. Clarifies board committee powers, share issuance procedures, and dissolution voting thresholds. Non-controversial business law update.
supporters: Washington State Bar Association, business attorneys, corporations
watchers: Corporate secretaries, compliance officers, business lawyers
fullSummary: Non-controversial technical bill updating corporate statutes. Passed with broad bipartisan support. Recommended by WSBA Business Law Section. Brings Washington law in line with national trends. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning parental rights by modifying provisions related to student medical records and school policies.
summary: Modifies voter-approved parental rights initiative (I-2081). Removes parental access to student medical records, allows schools to delay responses to inquiries, and mandates transgender policy alignment with state standards.
supporters: Education groups, LGBTQ advocates, student privacy advocates
opponents: Parent rights groups, conservative organizations, Let’s Go Washington
fullSummary: Highly controversial bill that modifies voter-approved parental rights law. Democrats argue it protects student privacy and LGBTQ students; Republicans call it subverting voter will. Legal challenges expected. School districts face compliance deadline of September 2025.
